nc_main_tier.blurb: The Main Tier is the central stretch of Ship Rock, a steep trad cliff beside the Blue Ridge Parkway south of Boone. Nearly everything here is protected by gear, with only a couple of bolted lines, and a lead is expected. The climbing leans toward the 5.10 and 5.11 range, with a smaller group of 5.12 and 5.13 and a handful of easier lines. At this elevation the cliff stays cooler than the Piedmont, which is why climbers from lower down come up in spring, summer and fall. Getting down means rappelling from the anchors at the top of the routes, and some stations need two raps or two ropes. The ground below is fragile, so stick to the worn climbers' trails.

nc_middle_hawksbill.blurb: Middle Hawksbill is the central of three cliff bands on Hawksbill Mountain, on the east rim of Linville Gorge. It holds a mix of trad and sport lines, mostly steep and sustained, and the grades cluster from 5.10 through 5.12 with a few 5.13s and only a handful of easier climbs. Climbers who come here usually expect a good pump. The wall looks out over the gorge to the southwest, and a long low roof marks the far right end. It is a short hike from the trailhead, but this is wilderness country, so plan on self-reliance.
nc_middle_hawksbill.parking_note: Reach it from NC 181 by way of Gingercake Road, then bear left onto Table Rock Road (USFS 210). Pavement gives out in under a mile; stay on the gravel for roughly 1.7 miles more and the signed Hawksbill trailhead appears on your left.
nc_middle_hawksbill.approach: Walk up the Hawksbill trail to a sharp uphill left bend, follow the summit trail for a few minutes, then take the climbers' trail that peels off to the right toward the Upper wall. Middle Hawksbill lies about 400 yards farther down that path.

nc_south_side_2.blurb: The South Side of Looking Glass Rock is a trad sector with something for most climbers, from easy fifth-class lines in the 5.5 range up to hard test pieces. The bulk of the climbs fall between 5.8 and 5.10. Many routes are multi-pitch, route-finding is mostly straightforward, and bolted rappel stations give plenty of ways down. Because it faces south, it catches sun through the day, which suits cooler months. Expect a steady uphill hike to the base before you rack up.

nc_cereal_buttress.blurb: Cereal Buttress is among the busiest sectors at Rumbling Bald, the gneiss crag near Chimney Rock that is best known as a winter destination. Crack climbing dominates, from moderate lines upward, and a few routes run more than one pitch. Most of the climbs are trad, with a scattering of sport and top-rope lines. Grades are weighted toward 5.11, with a solid spread of 5.8 to 5.10 as well. It takes a walk to reach, and the cracks here are mostly meant to be led.
nc_cereal_buttress.approach: From the parking area, follow the rutted old jeep road for about three quarters of a mile as it narrows to a trail, then continue past the boulderfield. At the fork, bear right for the main buttress and the Cereal Wall, or left for the left end and the Comatose zone.

nc_amphitheater.blurb: The Amphitheater is a bowl of cliffs on the east rim of Linville Gorge, curving into a rough semicircle with a small pass in the middle. It is a remote, traditional area: nearly all the climbing is on gear, with one aid line, and grades run from low fifth class through the 5.9s with a few at 5.11. Reaching the base means a steep, rough descent that takes real scrambling confidence, and the paths down are unofficial and patchy. Rescue is slow in the gorge, so bring route-finding skills and be self-sufficient. The viewpoint above looks down the gorge toward Shortoff Mountain.

nc_06_red_wall.blurb: Red Wall is one of the main climbing areas at Crowders Mountain, a quartzite ridge in a state park about 30 miles west of Charlotte. It offers a mix of trad and sport, and the grades center on 5.8 with a good number of 5.9 through 5.12. The park as a whole has a lot of top-rope options and an easy approach, but dense foliage can make finding sun a chore. Resurgence Walls, a further group of steep faces, lie just down and to the right of Red Wall.

nt_twin_falls_gorge_territorial_park_ice.blurb: Twin Falls Gorge is a steep canyon on the Hay River in the Northwest Territories with two big waterfalls, and the rock is poor, so this is an ice destination. Most of the flows are WI2 to WI4, led by a good run of WI3, with one WI5 and a single M3 mixed line. The canyon breaks into zones running west to east, from Alexandra Falls through the Main Flows and the Oxbows to Escarpment Creek, and it is still being explored. The Alexandra Falls end sits in shade through winter and spring, so it is the last to build up. Expect cold, remote conditions and a long way from services.
nt_twin_falls_gorge_territorial_park_ice.parking_note: Drive Highway 1 to just beyond Enterprise. The Louise Falls entrance, plowed most of the winter, is the handiest place to leave a car, closest to the densest ice. The Alexandra Falls pull-off is cleared too but sits far from most of the routes.

ns_sorrow_s_end_2.blurb: Sorrow's End is a short, sheer granite cliff above Shellbird Lake in the Terence Bay barrens near Halifax, standing out from the flat country around it. It has a fairly even mix of trad and sport, plus some top-rope lines. Grades start around 5.7 and the weight sits in the 5.8 and the 5.10 to 5.11 range, with a few 5.12 and 5.13 sport climbs. The exposure keeps bugs down, but in summer the sun reaches the wall around midday and it gets hot; the lake is close enough to cool off in afterward.
ns_sorrow_s_end_2.parking_note: Turn off Terence Bay Road onto the dirt Nice View Drive and follow it to the end, where you can pull in. It serves homes, so keep the way clear for residents.
ns_sorrow_s_end_2.approach: Start on the easy-to-spot ATV track and branch onto a narrow footpath that leads toward the cliff. Many trails criss-cross the barrens and some end in swampy ground, so carry a map or compass. Boots that handle mud help in spring.

oh_amusement_wall.blurb: Amusement Wall is a section of the Southeast sector, nicknamed the Darkside, at Mad River Gorge near Springfield, Ohio's largest climbing area. Bouldering makes up most of the climbing here, with problems ranging from V0 up to V9 and a clump of V3 to V5, along with a smaller set of bolted sport lines mostly around 5.10. The sector sits under a thick tree canopy and stays cool in warm weather. Wet trails can be slippery on the walk in.
